<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t.main.mfd}
Let $2\leq n+1\leq10$ and let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold with boundary. Let $S\subset\partial M$ be relatively open, and let $M'\Subset M\cup S$. Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $0<b<1$. For every $\Lambda>0$, there are constants $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $C<\infty$ with the following property.

Suppose that $0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0$ and that $u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(M\cup S,(-1,1))$ is stable in $M\cup S$ and satisfies
\[
\varepsilon^2\Delta_\mathrm{g} u_\varepsilon=W'(u_\varepsilon)\quad\text{in }M,
\qquad \partial_\nu u_\varepsilon=0\quad\text{on }S,
\]
together with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C11-estimate-main}
|\mathcal A(u_\varepsilon)|\leq\Lambda
\quad\text{on }\{|u_\varepsilon|\leq1-b\}\cap\{|\nabla u_\varepsilon|\neq0\}.
\end{equation}
Then every component $\Gamma$ of $\{u_\varepsilon=0\}$ meeting $S$ satisfies 
\begin{equation}\label{e.mc.rates}
\|H_\Gamma\|_{L^\infty(\Gamma\cap M')}
\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^2,
\qquad
[H_\Gamma]_{C^\theta(\Gamma\cap M')}
\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^2,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C2,theta-main}
\|\mathrm{I\!I}_\Gamma\|_{C^\theta(\Gamma\cap M')}\leq C,
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{I\!I}_\Gamma$ denotes the second fundamental form of the hypersurface $\Gamma$, and $H_\Gamma$ its mean curvature.
The constants depend only on $M'$, the fixed geometry near $M'$, $W$, $b$, $\theta$, and $\Lambda$, and are independent of the number of transition layers.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{e.dim.2}
Notice that, if $n+1=2$, then the level set $\{u_\varepsilon=0\}$ is a union of embedded curves, and the norm of its second fundamental form is simply the absolute value of its geodesic curvature $k_{\{u_\varepsilon=0\}}$, which is clearly the same as the mean curvature of $\{u_\varepsilon=0\}$. Therefore, in ambient dimension 2, \eqref{e.mc.rates} gives
\begin{equation}
    \|k_\Gamma\|_{L^\infty(\Gamma\cap M')}
\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^2,
\qquad
[k_\Gamma]_{C^\theta(\Gamma\cap M')}
\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^2,
\end{equation}
for every component $\Gamma$ of $\{u_\varepsilon=0\}$ meeting $S$. On the other hand, unlike in the interior case of \cite[Theorem 3.6]{wang-wei} and \cite[Proposition C.4]{chodosh-mantoulidis-2d}, it is not possible to obtain decay estimates (in $\varepsilon$) for the enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}(u_\varepsilon)$. Indeed, at a point $p\in \{u_\varepsilon=0\}\cap S$, by \eqref{|Anormsquare|2},
\[
|\mathcal A(u_\varepsilon)|^2=|k_{\{u_\varepsilon = 0\}}|^2+|\partial_\nu \log|\nabla u_\varepsilon||^2,
\]
and an easy computation (see Remark \ref{r.s11.enhanced.boundary}) gives $|\partial_\nu\log|\nabla u_\varepsilon||^2
 =|k_S|^2$, where $k_S$ denotes the geodesic curvature of the boundary at $p\in \{u_\varepsilon=0\}\cap S$. In particular, $k_S$ is independent of $\varepsilon$. See also Remark \ref{r.s11.boundary.dependence} for a more detailed discussion of this issue.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{r.intro.totally.geodesic}
If $S$ is totally geodesic on a neighbourhood of $M'\cap S$, the estimates improve and extend to all transition levels. More precisely, if $0<b<b'<1$, then uniformly for $t\in[-1+b',1-b']$, every component $\Gamma_t$ of $\{u_\varepsilon=t\}$ meeting $S$ satisfies, on $M'$,
\[
\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma_t}\|_{C^\theta}\leq C,
\qquad
\|H_{\Gamma_t}\|_{L^\infty}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|,
\qquad
[H_{\Gamma_t}]_{C^\theta}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|,
\]
where the constant $C$ (in addition to the geometry of $M'$, $W$, $b$ , $\theta$, $\Lambda$) also depends on $b'$.
If, in addition, $n+1=2$, then  
\[
|\mathcal A(u_\varepsilon)|\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|
\quad\text{on }M'\cap\{|u_\varepsilon|\leq1-b'\}.
\]
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{l.nab.u}
Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{t.main.mfd}, there are constants
$\varepsilon_\bullet>0$ and $c>0$, depending only on $b$, $\Lambda$, $W$, and the fixed
geometry near $M'$, such that, whenever $0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_\bullet$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.nab.u}
 \varepsilon|\nabla u_\varepsilon|\geq c
 \qquad\text{in }\{|u_\varepsilon|\leq1-b\}\cap M'.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The argument is similar to \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}. Let us assume by contradiction that there exist\ sequences $(u_{\varepsilon_i},\varepsilon_i)$ with\ $\varepsilon_i\rightarrow 0$, $p_i\in \{|u_{\varepsilon_i}|\leq 1-b\}\cap M'$ so that $u_{\varepsilon_i}\in C^{\infty}(M\cup S, (-1,1))$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_i$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $S$ and $\varepsilon_i|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_i}(p_i)|\rightarrow 0$. Let $d_i=d_\mathrm{g}(p_i,S)=d_\mathrm{g}(p_i, q_i)$, where $q_i\in S$ is the nearest point projection of $p_i$ to $S$; we need to consider two cases:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item either $\liminf_{i\rightarrow \infty}\varepsilon_i^{-1}d_i=\infty$, 
\item or $\liminf_{i\rightarrow \infty}\varepsilon_i^{-1}d_i<\infty$.
\end{enumerate}

Assume first that $d_i/\varepsilon_i\to\infty$. In geodesic normal coordinates centreed at
$p_i$, define
\[
 E_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}(v)=\exp_{p_i}(\varepsilon_i v),
 \qquad
 \mathrm{g}_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}=\varepsilon_i^{-2}E_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}^*\mathrm{g},
 \qquad
 \widetilde u_i=u_{\varepsilon_i}\circ E_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}.
\]
After identifying $T_{p_i}M'$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$  by choosing an orthonormal basis, the domain of $E_{p,\varepsilon}$ can be identified with $B_{\varepsilon^{-1}r}(0)$, where $r=\operatorname{inj}_p$. Then $\tilde{u}_i$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=1$ on $(B_{r_i}(0),\mathrm{g}_{p_i,\varepsilon_i})$, where $r_i=(2\varepsilon_i)^{-1}\min\{d_i, \operatorname{inj}_{p_i}\}$, $|\tilde{u}_i(0)|\leq 1-b$, $|\nabla \tilde{u}_i(0)|\rightarrow 0$ and $\mathrm{g}_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}$ converges to the Euclidean metric\ in $C^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$. Hence, by elliptic estimates, $\tilde{u}_i$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$. Therefore, there exists\ $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$, a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, such that\ up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_i\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{2}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$. Since $|\tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|\leq 1-b$, $|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|= 0$, $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is non-constant. As in \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}, by \eqref{e.esff.bd}, we have $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b\}\cap \{|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$. By the unique continuation principle (for example see \cite{jerison1985unique}) for the linear equation $\Delta \partial_{i}\tilde{u}_{\infty}=W'(\tilde{u}_{\infty})\partial_{i}\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ ($i=1, \dots, n+1$) and Lebesgue's density theorem, the critical set $\{\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}=0\}$ has zero Lebesgue measure. By \eqref{|Anormsquare|2} and $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\varepsilon})|\leq \Lambda \varepsilon$ (which follows from \eqref{e.esff.bd}), we conclude that $\{\tilde{u}_{\infty}=t\}$ is a flat hyperplane for almost every $t\in[-1+b, 1-b]$.  This implies that $\tilde{u}_{\infty}=U(x\cdot e)$, where $U: \mathbb{R}\to [-1, 1]$ is a nonconstant stable entire solution of the 1-dimensional Allen--Cahn equation and $e$ is a  unit vector. In particular, $U$ must be the 1-dimensional heteroclinic solution $\mathbb{H}$, which implies that $|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|\neq 0$. Thus we arrive at a contradiction.

Assume now $\liminf_{i\rightarrow \infty}\varepsilon_i^{-1}d_i<\infty$, there exists\ $d\geq 0$ such that,\ possibly after passing to a subsequence, $\lim_{i\rightarrow \infty}\varepsilon_i^{-1}d_i=d$. In boundary Fermi coordinates centreed at $q_i$, define
\[
 E_{q_i,\varepsilon_i}(x_1,x')
 =\exp^M_{\exp^{\partial M}_{q_i}(\varepsilon_i x')}
 \!\left(\varepsilon_i x_1\nu_{\partial M}
 \bigl(\exp^{\partial M}_{q_i}(\varepsilon_i x')\bigr)\right),
 \qquad
 \mathrm{g}_{q_i,\varepsilon_i}=\varepsilon_i^{-2}E_{q_i,\varepsilon_i}^*\mathrm{g}.
\]
These coordinates map $\{x_1=0\}$ exactly to $\partial M$.  Thus
$\widetilde u_i=u_{\varepsilon_i}\circ E_{q_i,\varepsilon_i}$ satisfies the homogeneous
Neumann condition on the flat boundary, the metrics converge smoothly to the Euclidean metric
on $\mathbb R^{n+1}_+$, and the preimages of $p_i$ remain in a fixed compact set. Then there is a fixed $r>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $i$ the normal exponential map of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $B^{\partial M}_r(q_i)\times[0,r)$.
In particular, $\tilde{u}_i$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=1$ on $(B^+_{r_i}(0),\mathrm{g}_{q_i,\varepsilon_i})$, where $r_i=(2\varepsilon_i)^{-1}\min\{d(q_i,\partial M\setminus S), r\}$, and it satisfies the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial_0B^+_{r_i}(0)$. Moreover, if $\tilde{p}_i=E_{q_i,\varepsilon_i}^{-1}(p_i)$, then $|\tilde{u}_i(\tilde{p}_i)|\leq 1-b$ and $|\nabla \tilde{u}_i(\tilde{p}_i)|\rightarrow 0$. Since $\mathrm{g}_{p_i,\varepsilon_i}$ converges to the Euclidean metric\ in $C^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$, $\tilde{u}_i$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$. Therefore,\ there exists\ $\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*$, a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+$, such that\ up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_i\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*$ in $C^{2}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$. Moreover, there exists\ $\tilde{p}_{\infty}$ such that\ up to a subsequence, $\tilde{p}_i \rightarrow \tilde{p}_{\infty}$; so $|\tilde{p}_{\infty}|=d$, $|\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|\leq 1-b$, $|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}^*(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|= 0$. Hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*$ is non-constant. We define  $\tilde{u}_{\infty}\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ by
\begin{equation}\label{e.even.refl}
\tilde{u}_{\infty}(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{n+1})=
\begin{cases}	
\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{n+1}) &\text{ when } x_1\geq 0;\\
\tilde{u}_{\infty}^*(-x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{n+1}) &\text{ when } x_1\leq 0.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Then $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} with\ $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Since $u_{\varepsilon_i}$ satisfies \eqref{e.esff.bd}, arguing as in \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}, we conclude that $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b\}\cap \{|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$.  Similarly to the previous case, by unique continuation and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is again of the form $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(x)=\mathbb{H}(x\cdot e)$ for some unit vector $e$. Hence $|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|\neq 0$. Thus we arrive again at a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{l.Fermi.coord}\cite[Lemma A.2]{LZ}
There exist\ constants $r_1$ and $\{\mathsf{C}_m\}_{m=0}^\infty$ depending only on the metric\ \(\mathrm{g}\) and $S'$ such that\ the following holds. Let $\mathrm{g}_{ij}$, $\bar{\Gamma}_{ij}^k$ denote the components of $\mathrm{g}$ and the Christoffel symbols in a Fermi coordinate system centreed at $p$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{e.g.Ga.0}
\mathrm{g}_{11}=1,\quad \mathrm{g}_{1i}=0,\quad\bar{\Gamma}_{i1}^1=\bar{\Gamma}_{11}^i=\bar{\Gamma}_{11}^1=0\quad \forall i\geq 2
\end{equation}
and for all $1 \le i, j \le n+1$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.g.Ga.est}
\left|\mathrm{g}_{ij}(x)-\delta_{ij}\right|\leq C_0\bar{r}_p(x)\text{ on }\mathcal{B}_{r_1}(p),\quad \|\mathrm{g}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\|_{C^m(\mathcal{B}_{r_1}(p))}\leq \mathsf{C}_m\; \forall\; m \ge 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{t.main.ball}
Assume $2\leq n+1\leq10$. Let $B_3^+(0)$ be equipped with a smooth Riemannian metric $\hat{g}$ so that the following conditions are satisfied. 
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\partial_{x_1}$ is the inward pointing unit normal along $\partial_0B_3^+(0)$.
	\item If $\hat{g}_{ij}$, $\hat{\Gamma}_{ij}^k$ denote the components of $\hat{g}$ and its Christoffel symbols, then, for every fixed $m$,
	\begin{align}
	&\hat{g}_{11}=1,\quad \hat{g}_{1i}=0,\quad\hat{\Gamma}_{i1}^1=\hat{\Gamma}_{11}^i=\hat{\Gamma}_{11}^1=0\quad \forall i\geq 2,\label{e.g.Ga.0.ball}\\
	&\hat{g}_{ij}(0)=\delta_{ij}\quad \left\|\hat{g}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\right\|_{C^m(B_3^+(0))}\leq \eta_0\label{e.g.Ga.est.ball}.
	\end{align}
\end{itemize}
Fix $\theta\in (0, 1)$ and $0<b<1$. There exist constants $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $C_0<\infty$, depending only on $n,\theta,b,W,c_0,\eta_0$, and $\Lambda_0$, such that the following holds. Suppose $0<\varepsilon\leq \varepsilon_0$, $u_{\varepsilon}:(B_3^+(0),\hat{g})\rightarrow (-1,1)$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.AC} satisfying the following conditions.

\noindent(H1) $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies the vanishing Neumann boundary condition $\partial_{x_1}u_\varepsilon=0$ along $\partial_0B_3^+(0)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{e.nab.u.ball}
\varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\geq c_0 \text{ on }\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b\}.
\end{equation}

\noindent(H2) Let $\hat{\Xi}$ denote the union of all the connected components of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}\cap \left(\mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0)\times (-2,2)\right)$ which have non-empty intersections with $\mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0)\times (-1.5,1.5)$. Then $\hat{\Xi}$ can be written as a union of graphs
\[\hat{\Xi}=\bigcup_{\alpha}\{x_{n+1}=\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x'):x'=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in \mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0)\}\]
where $\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0),(-1.6,1.6))$ with\ $\partial_{x_1} \hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon} = 0 \text{ along } \partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0)$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.na.ftl}
|\nabla\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}|\leq \eta_0,\; |\nabla^2\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}|\leq \Lambda_0 \text{ on }\mathbb{B}^+_{2}(0).
\end{equation}

\noindent(H3) We have \begin{equation}\label{e.esff.bd.ball}
|\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|\leq \Lambda_0 \quad \text{in}\,\,\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1- b\}\cap \{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\not=0\}.
\end{equation}

Then every component of $\hat\Xi$ satisfies, on $B_{1/2}^+(0)$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.main.ball.zero.II}
 \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\{u_\varepsilon=0\}}\|_{C^\theta}\leq C_0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{e.mn.curv.ball}
 \|H_{\{u_\varepsilon=0\}}\|_{L^\infty}
 \leq C_0\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^2,
 \qquad
 [H_{\{u_\varepsilon=0\}}]_{C^\theta}
 \leq C_0\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The constants $\eta_0$ and $\Lambda_0$ in \eqref{e.g.Ga.est.ball}, \eqref{e.nab.u.ball}, \eqref{e.na.ftl} and \eqref{e.esff.bd.ball} are fixed before $\varepsilon_0$ is chosen and will be assumed to be sufficiently small.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
If, in addition, $\partial_0B_3^+(0)$ is totally geodesic and $0<b<b'<1$, then, uniformly for
$t\in[-1+b',1-b']$, every corresponding graphical component of
$\{u_\varepsilon=t\}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{e.main.ball.all.II}
 \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\{u_\varepsilon=t\}}\|_{C^\theta(B_{1/2}^+(0))}\leq C_0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{e.main.ball.all.H}
 \|H_{\{u_\varepsilon=t\}}\|_{L^\infty(B_{1/2}^+(0))}
 \leq C_0\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|,
 \qquad
 [H_{\{u_\varepsilon=t\}}]_{C^\theta(B_{1/2}^+(0))}
 \leq C_0\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|.
\end{equation}
where $C_0$ also depends on $b'$ (in addition to $n,\theta,b,W,c_0,\eta_0$, and $\Lambda_0$).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{l.grad.A}
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{A=O(e)}
    |\nabla^k \mathcal{A}|=O(\varepsilon)
\end{equation}
on $B^+_{3R-1}(0)\cap \{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ for all\ $k\geq 0$. As a consequence, if $x\in \{|u|\leq 1-b'\}$ and $\Sigma = \{u=u(x)\}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{e.grad.sff}
|\nabla_{\Sigma}^k\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma}|=O(\varepsilon) \qquad \text{on } \Sigma\cap B^+_{3R-1}(0) \ \  \forall  k\geq 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See Appendix \ref{Agradient} for the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{l.exp.map}
	For all $(x,v)\in \mathcal{S}$ and indices $i,j$, there holds
	\begin{equation}
		|\partial_{x_i}\mathscr{E}^j(x,v) - \delta_{ij}|+ |\partial_{v_i}\mathscr{E}^j(x,v) - \delta_{ij}|\lesssim \varepsilon|v|,\quad |D^m \mathscr{E}^i(x,v)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|v|)\; \forall  m\geq 2.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The proof is similar to \cite[Proposition A.1]{KapouleasLi21}. Since $\mathscr{E}(x,v)= \Phi_1(1,x,v)$, we are going to restrict $\Phi$ on $[0,1]\times \mathcal{S}$ in this proof. Differentiating \eqref{e.Ph} we obtain
 	\begin{align}\label{e.Ph1}
 	\partial_s\partial_{*}\Phi_1^k=\partial_{*}\Phi_2^k, \qquad \partial_s \partial_{*}\Phi_2^k=-\sum_{ijl}\partial_{x_l}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\Phi_1)\partial_{*}\Phi_1^l\Phi_2^i\Phi_2^j-2\sum_{ij}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\Phi_1)\partial_{*}\Phi_2^i\Phi_2^j,
 	\end{align}
where $\partial_{*}$ is any element in $\{\partial_{x_i},\partial_{v_i}:i=1,\dots,n+1\}$. We note that $\Phi(0,x,v)=(x,v)$, $|\Phi_2(s,x,v)|=|v|$ and (since the metric\ $\tilde{g}$ is uniformly close to the Euclidean metric) $\varepsilon|v|=O(1)$ for all\ $(x,v)\in \mathcal{S}$. Therefore, using Gronwall's inequality for vector valued functions \cite[Theorem D.2]{Lee}, we conclude that $|\partial_{*}\Phi(s,x,v)|$ is uniformly bounded for $(s,x,v)\in [0,1]\times \mathcal{S}$. Using this, one can deduce from \eqref{e.Ph1} that $|\partial_s\partial_{*}\Phi_2^k|\lesssim \varepsilon |v|$ and
$|\partial_{*}\Phi_1^k(1,x,v)-\partial_{*}\Phi_1^k(0,x,v)-\partial_{*}\Phi_2^k(0,x,v)|\lesssim \varepsilon|v|.$
This implies the $C^1$ estimate for $\mathscr{E}$.

Differentiating \eqref{e.Ph1} we obtain
\begin{align}\label{e.Ph2}
\begin{split}
    &\partial_s\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_1^k=\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_2^k,\\
&\partial_s \partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_2^k=-\sum_{ijl}\partial_{x_l}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\Phi_1)\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_1^l\Phi_2^i\Phi_2^j-2\sum_{ij}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\Phi_1)\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_2^i\Phi_2^j+\mathcal{E}
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $\partial_{\circ}$ is any element in $\{\partial_{x_i},\partial_{v_i}:i=1,\dots,n+1\}$ and $|\mathcal{E}|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|v|).$ Note that $\mathcal{E}$ does not contain any second order derivatives of $\Phi$. Therefore, using Gronwall's inequality for vector valued functions \cite[Theorem D.2]{Lee}, we obtain that $|\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi(s,x,v)|$ is uniformly bounded for $(s,x,v)\in [0,1]\times \mathcal{S}$. Using this, one can deduce from \eqref{e.Ph2} that $|\partial_s\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_2^k|\lesssim \varepsilon (1+|v|)$, which implies $|\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_1^k|\lesssim \varepsilon (1+|v|)$. Thus we obtain the $C^2$ estimate for $\mathscr{E}$ and the higher order estimates can be proved in a similar way.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
In what follows, we will denote by $\nabla$ the gradient of a scalar map, while $D$ will be used for the gradient of vector valued maps, i.e. the gradient of each component. Furthermore, everything will be computed in the ambient coordinates $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n + 1})$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{l.tilde.t.Pi}
	There exists $\tilde\delta>0$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that\ the following holds.
	\begin{equation}\label{e.tilde.t.Pi}
	|D\tilde{\Pi}|=O(1),\quad |\nabla^m\tilde{t}|+|D^m\tilde{\Pi}|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tilde{t}|) \quad \text{ on }\{|\tilde{t}|\leq \tilde\delta R\}\;\forall m\geq 2.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}:\tilde{\Sigma}\times (-\tilde\delta R, \tilde\delta R)\to \mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)$ be defined by $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z})=\exp_y(\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))=\mathscr{E}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))$, where $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit normal along $\tilde{\Sigma}$ satisfying $\langle  \mathbf{n} , \partial_{x_{n+1}}\rangle>0$, and $\tilde\delta>0$ will be determined later in the proof. We note that if $y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in \tilde{\Sigma}$, then $x_i(y)=y_i$ if $1\leq i\leq n$ and $x_{n+1}(y)=\tilde{f}(y_1,\dots, y_n)$. Hence
\begin{align}\label{e.tilde.E}
\begin{split}
\partial_{y_j}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^i(y,\tilde{z}) &=\partial_{x_j}\mathscr{E}^i(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))+\partial_{x_{n+1}}\mathscr{E}^i(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\partial_{x_j}f(y_1,\dots,y_n)\\
& +\sum_k\tilde{z}\partial_{v_k}\mathscr{E}^i(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\partial_{y_j}\mathbf{n}^k(y),\\
\partial_{\tilde{z}}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^i(y,\tilde{z}) &= \sum_k\partial_{v_k}\mathscr{E}^i(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\mathbf{n}^k(y).
\end{split} 
\end{align}
Therefore, by Lemma \ref{l.exp.map} and \eqref{e.na.f}, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{e.del.tilde.E}
|\partial_{y_j}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^i(y,\tilde{z})-\delta_{ij}|\lesssim \varepsilon|\tilde{z}|+\eta_0,\;1\leq i,j\leq n+1,
\end{equation}
where $\partial_{y_{n+1}}$ stands for $\partial_{\tilde{z}}$. This implies that if $\delta$ and $\eta_0$ are sufficiently small, the Jacobian of  $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}$ is greater or equal than $1/2$. Differentiating \eqref{e.tilde.E} and using Lemma \ref{l.exp.map}, one can show that
\begin{equation}\label{e.D^k.tilde.E}
|D^m\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z})|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tilde{z}|)\;\forall m\geq 2.
\end{equation}
Since $\tilde{t}(\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z}))=\tilde{z}$ and $\tilde{\Pi}(\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z}))=y$, using inverse function theorem, one can deduce from \eqref{e.del.tilde.E} and \eqref{e.D^k.tilde.E} that if $\tilde\delta$ and $\eta_0$ are sufficiently small,
\begin{equation}\label{e.tilde.t.Pi'}
|D\tilde{\Pi}|=O(1),\quad |\nabla^m\tilde{t}|+|D^m\tilde{\Pi}|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tilde{t}|) \text{ on }\{|\tilde{t}|\leq \tilde\delta R\}\;\forall m\geq 2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{l.vect.Z}
The vector field $Z$ has the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] $Z$ is tangential to $\partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{1.8R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)$.
	\item[(ii)] $Z=\tilde{Z}$ along $\Sigma$ and is perpendicular to $\Sigma$.
	\item[(iii)] $\langle Z, \tilde{Z}\rangle=1$.
	\item[(iv)] $(Z-\tilde{Z})$ is perpendicular to $\tilde{Z}$.
	\item[(v)] If $Z=\sum_iZ^i\partial_{x_i}$ then $|Z^i-\delta_{i,n+1}|\lesssim \eta_0+\Lambda_0$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{twisted fermi def}
Given a coordinate system $y=(y_1, \dots, y_n)$ on $\Sigma$,  \textit{twisted Fermi coordinates} on $\mathbb{B}^+_{1.8R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)$ with respect to $\Sigma$ are defined by $Y_{\Sigma}(y,z)=\Theta_{z}(y)$, for $y\in \Sigma$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{d.twisted.time.projection}
The twisted Fermi coordinate time function $t:\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and projection map $\Pi:\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R) \rightarrow \Sigma\cap (\mathbb{B}^+_{1.7R}(0)\times (-2R,2R))$ are defined by $t(p)=\tau_p$ and $\Pi(p)=\Theta(-t(p),p)$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Similar coordinate systems near a boundary point appear in \cite[Section 10]{Pacard-Ritore} and \cite[Definition 2.10]{KapouleasLi21}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{l.Fc.vs.tFc.1}
Let $p\in \mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)$. Then $\tilde{t}(p)=t(p)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $q=\Pi(p)$. We consider the function $\gamma(\tau)=\tilde{t}(\Theta(\tau,q))$. Then $\gamma(0)=0$ and by Lemma \ref{l.vect.Z}(iv), $\gamma'(\tau)=\left\langle \nabla \tilde{t}, Z\right\rangle(\Theta(\tau,q))=1$. Hence, $\tilde{t}(p)=\gamma(\tau_p)=\tau_p=t(p)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{l.Tht}
	Let us fix $K>0$. For all $(\tau,x)$ satisfying $|\tau|,|t(x)|\leq K\sqrt{R}$ and for all indices $i,j$, there holds
	\begin{align}
	&|\partial_{x_i}\Theta^j(\tau,x) - \delta_{ij}|\lesssim \varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^2+|t(x)|^2),\\ 
& |D^m_x \Theta^i(\tau,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(|\tau|+\tau^2+t(x)^2),\qquad |D^m \Theta^i(\tau,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tau|^2+|t(x)|^2)\; \forall  m\geq 2.
	\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{l.exp.map}. Differentiating \eqref{e.Tht} we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{e.del.x.Tht}
\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_i}\Theta^k=\sum_p\partial_{x_p}Z^k(\Theta)\partial_{x_i}\Theta^p.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, \eqref{e.na.Z} implies
$|\nabla^mZ(\Theta(\tau,x))|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|)$ for all $m\geq 1$.
Therefore, using Gronwall's inequality for vector valued functions \cite[Theorem D.2]{Lee}, we conclude that $|\partial_{x_i}\Theta^k|=O(1)$. Using this estimate, we deduce from \eqref{e.del.x.Tht} that 
\begin{equation}\label{e.del2.ta.x.Tht}
|\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_i}\Theta^k(\tau,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|),
\end{equation}
hence
\begin{equation}
|\partial_{x_i}\Theta^k(\tau,x)-\partial_{x_i}\Theta^k(0,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^2+|t(x)|^2).
\end{equation}
This implies the $C^1$ estimate for $\Theta$. 

Differentiating \eqref{e.del.x.Tht}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{e.del2.x.Tht}
\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_ix_j}\Theta^k=\sum_{p,q}\partial_{x_px_q}Z^k(\Theta)\partial_{x_i}\Theta^p\partial_{x_j}\Theta^q+\sum_p\partial_{x_p}Z^k(\Theta)\partial_{x_ix_j}\Theta^p.
\end{equation}
Therefore, using Gronwall's inequality for vector valued functions \cite[Theorem D.2]{Lee}, we conclude that $|\partial_{x_ix_j}\Theta^k|=O(1)$. Using this estimate, we deduce from \eqref{e.del2.x.Tht} that 
\begin{equation}
|\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_ix_j}\Theta^k(\tau,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|);
\end{equation}
hence
\begin{equation}\label{e.est.del2.x.Tht}
|\partial_{x_ix_j}\Theta^k(\tau,x)|\lesssim \varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^2+|t(x)|^2).
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{e.del2.ta.x.Tht} and \eqref{e.est.del2.x.Tht}, we obtain the $C^2$ estimates for $\Theta$. Higher order estimates can be proved in a similar way.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{l.t.Pi}
There exists $0<\delta<\tilde{\delta}$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that\ the following holds.
	\begin{equation}\label{e.t.Pi}
	|D\Pi|=O(1),\quad |\nabla^m t|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|),\quad |D^m \Pi|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2) \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta \sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 2.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The estimates for $|\nabla^m t|$ follow from Lemma \ref{l.tilde.t.Pi} and Lemma \ref{l.Fc.vs.tFc.1}. Let $\hat{\Theta}$ denote the restriction of $\Theta$ on $[-\delta \sqrt{R}, \delta \sqrt{R}]\times \Sigma$, where $\delta\in(0,\tilde\delta)$ is to be determined. We note that if $y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in \Sigma$, then $x_i(y)=y_i$ if $1\leq i\leq n$ and $x_{n+1}(y)=f(y_1,\dots, y_n)$. Hence
\begin{align}\label{e.hat.Tht}
& \partial_{y_i} \hat{\Theta}^j(z,y)=\partial_{x_i}\Theta^j(z,y)+\partial_{x_{n+1}}\Theta^j(z,y)\partial_{x_i}f(y_1,\dots,y_n),\\
& \partial_z \hat{\Theta}^j(z,y)=Z^j(\Theta(z,y)).
\end{align}
Therefore, by Lemma \ref{l.Tht}, \eqref{e.na.f} and Lemma \ref{l.vect.Z}(v), as $(\delta+\eta_0+\Lambda_0)\to 0$ we infer 
\begin{equation}\label{e.del.hat.Tht}
|\partial_{y_i}\hat{\Theta}^j(z,y)-\delta_{ij}|=o(1),\;1\leq i,j\leq n+1,
\end{equation}
where $\partial_{y_{n+1}}$ stands for $\partial_{z}$. This implies if $\delta,\;\eta_0,\;\Lambda_0$ are sufficiently small, the Jacobian of  $\hat{\Theta}$ is greater or equal than $1/2$. Differentiating \eqref{e.hat.Tht} and using Lemma \ref{l.Tht}, one can show that
\begin{equation}\label{e.D^k.hat.Tht}
|D^m\hat{\Theta}(z,y)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2)\;\forall m\geq 2.
\end{equation}
Since $t(\hat{\Theta}(z,y))=z$ and $\Pi(\hat{\Theta}(z,y))=y$, using inverse function theorem, one can deduce from \eqref{e.del.hat.Tht} and \eqref{e.D^k.hat.Tht} that if $\delta,\;\eta_0,\;\Lambda_0$ are sufficiently small,
\begin{equation}\label{e.D.t.Pi}
|D\Pi|=O(1),\quad |D^m \Pi|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2) \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta \sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{l.na.y_i}
The following estimates hold  for $\partial_{y_i}$ and its covariant derivatives
\begin{align}
    \label{e.del.y_i.O(1)}
	|\partial_{y_i}| = O(1)  &\text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta\sqrt{R}\},\\
 \label{e.na.y_i}
	|\nabla^m\partial_{y_i}|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2) &\text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta\sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 1. 
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The lemma follows from \eqref{e.del_y_i} and Lemma \ref{l.Tht}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{l.del.y_1.t_be}
The following estimate holds
\begin{equation}\label{e.del.x_1-del.y_1}
	|\partial_{x_1}\varphi(y, z)-\partial_{y_1}\varphi(y, z)|\lesssim \varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)|\nabla \varphi(y, z)|\text{ on }\partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times [-\delta\sqrt R,\delta\sqrt R]
\end{equation}
for any smooth function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Notice that along $\partial_0\Sigma$, $\partial_{x_1}f=0$ by the setup in \ref{ss.twisted.Fermi.setup}, and $\partial_{x_1}=\partial_{y_1}$ by the definition of twisted Fermi coordinates. Hence, by \eqref{e.del_y_i}, on $\partial_0\{|z|\leq K\sqrt R |\}$
\begin{equation}
   \partial_{y_1}|_{(y,z)}=\sum_j\partial_{x_1}\Theta^j(z,y)\partial_{x_j}|_{(y,z)}.            
\end{equation}
Then \eqref{e.del.x_1-del.y_1} follows directly from Lemma \ref{l.Tht}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{l.Fc.vs.tFc.2}
	There exists\ $\delta >0$ such that\ the following holds: 
	$$d_{\Sigma}\left(\tilde{\Pi}(p),\Pi(p)\right)\lesssim \varepsilon (|t(p)|^2+|t(p)|^3) \text{ on } \{|t|\leq \delta R\}.$$
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $q=\Pi(p)$. We consider the function $G(\tau)=(\tilde{\Pi}_1(\Theta(\tau,q)),\dots, \tilde{\Pi}_n(\Theta(\tau,q)))$, where $\tilde{\Pi}_i=y_i\circ \tilde{\Pi}$. Then $G(0)=(y_1(q),\dots,y_n(q))$,
	\[\frac{d}{d\tau}\tilde{\Pi}(\Theta(\tau,q))=D\tilde{\Pi}(\Theta(\tau,q))(Z(\Theta(\tau,q))).\]
	Note that $\tilde{\Pi}$ is constant along the integral curves of $\tilde{Z}$. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{l.vect.Z}(ii), $G'(0)=(0,\dots,0)$. By Lemma \ref{l.tilde.t.Pi} and \eqref{e.na.Z}, $\left|G''(\tau)\right|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|\tau|)$. Therefore,\ by Taylor's theorem,  $$d_{\Sigma}\left(\tilde{\Pi}(p),\Pi(p)\right)\lesssim |G(t(p))-G(0)|\lesssim\varepsilon(|t(p)|^{2}+|t(p)|^3).$$
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{l.Z.Z-tld}
	There holds
	$$|Z-\tilde{Z}|\lesssim \varepsilon(|z|+z^2),\quad  |\nabla^m (Z-\tilde{Z})|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|) \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta R\}\;\forall m\geq 1.$$
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{r.tZ-Z}
    By Lemma \ref{l.vect.Z} (iv),
\begin{equation}\label{e.decomp.tZ}
	\partial_{\tilde{z}}=\partial_z-T=\partial_z-\sum_{i=1}^{n}T^i\partial_{y_i}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{l.Z.Z-tld}, for each index $i$, we have estimates
\begin{equation}\label{e.difference.z.tz}
	|T^i|\lesssim \varepsilon(|z|+z^2),\quad |\nabla^m T^i|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|) \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta R\}\;\forall m\geq 1.
\end{equation}
Notice that $T^i(y,z)=-g^{iz}(y,z)$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{l.dz(nu)}
	Let $J:\partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R)\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $J=\partial_{x_1}t=dz(\nu)$, $w(y)=\partial_z J(y,0)$ and $\tilde{J}(y,z)=J(y,z)-w(y)z$. Then
	\begin{equation}\label{e.dz(nu).1}
		|J|=|\partial_{\nu} z|\lesssim \varepsilon|z|(1+|z|+|z|^2) \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta \sqrt R\}.
	\end{equation} 
	Moreover,
	\begin{equation}\label{e.w.1}
		|\nabla^k w|=O(\varepsilon)\text{ on } \partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0) \;\forall k\geq 0,
	\end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation}\label{e.w.2}
		|\nabla^k_y \tilde{J}|\lesssim \varepsilon^2(1+|z|^3)z^2 \text{ on }\{|z|\leq \delta\sqrt R\}\;\forall k\geq 0.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{l.Fc.vs.tFc.1}, $\nabla t=\widetilde Z$, and hence
$J=\langle\widetilde Z,\nu\rangle$.  The sheet meets the boundary orthogonally, so
$J(y,0)=0$.  Since $\partial_z=Z$ and the integral curves of $\widetilde Z$ are unit-speed geodesics,
\begin{equation}\label{e.partial.z.J}
 \partial_zJ
 =\langle\nabla_{Z-\widetilde Z}\widetilde Z,\nu\rangle
  +\langle\widetilde Z,\nabla_Z\nu\rangle.
\end{equation}
With the sign convention of Section \ref{s.basic.definitions},
$\langle X,\nabla_Y\nu\rangle=-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_0}(Y,X)$ for vectors tangent to the boundary.
At $z=0$, where $Z=\widetilde Z$, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{e.w.boundary.geometry}
 w(y)=\partial_zJ(y,0)=-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_0}(\widetilde Z,\widetilde Z)(y,0).
\end{equation}
In particular, \eqref{e.rescaled.bound.sff} and the tangential derivative bounds for $\widetilde Z$
imply \eqref{e.w.1}.

Differentiating \eqref{e.partial.z.J} once more in the $Z$-direction, and using
$\nabla_{\widetilde Z}\widetilde Z=0$, expresses $\partial_{zz}J$ as a sum of contractions of
$\nabla^3t$, $\nabla^2t$, $Z-\widetilde Z$, $\nabla(Z-\widetilde Z)$,
$\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_0}$, and $\nabla\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_0}$.  Lemmas \ref{l.t.Pi} and
\ref{l.Z.Z-tld}, together with \eqref{e.rescaled.bound.sff}, therefore give
\begin{equation}\label{e.est.partial.zz.J}
 |\nabla_y^k\partial_{zz}J(y,z)|
 \lesssim_k \varepsilon^2(1+|z|^3)
 \qquad (|z|\leq\delta\sqrt R)
\end{equation}
for every fixed $k$.  The same differentiated identity, with one fewer $z$-derivative, gives
$|\nabla_y^k\partial_zJ|\lesssim_k\varepsilon(1+|z|+|z|^2)$.
Taylor's theorem at $z=0$, using $J(y,0)=0$ and the definition of $w$, now yields
\eqref{e.dz(nu).1} and
\[
 |\nabla_y^k(J(y,z)-w(y)z)|
 \leq |z|^2\sup_{|s|\leq|z|}|\nabla_y^k\partial_{zz}J(y,s)|,
\]
which is exactly \eqref{e.w.2}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{l.g^zz.twisted}
	In twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_\alpha$, $g^{zz}(y,z)=1$
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This follows from Lemma \ref{l.Fc.vs.tFc.1}. Indeed, $1=|\nabla\tilde{t}|^2=|\nabla t|^2=g^{zz}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{geometric approximation}
	Let $g_{\alpha}(y,z),\;\Gamma_{\alpha}(y,z),$ $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha}(y,z),\; H_{\alpha}(y,z)$ respectively denote the induced metric\ on $\Sigma_{\alpha, z}$, the second fundamental form of $\Sigma_{\alpha, z}$ and the mean curvature of $\Sigma_{\alpha, z}$ at $(y,z)$. For each  fixed $K>0$, if $z\in(-K |\log \varepsilon|, K|\log \varepsilon|)$, we have for all $1\leq i,j,k,l\leq n$
	\begin{gather}\label{e.g_ij.approx}
		|g_{\alpha, ij}(y, z)-g_{\alpha,ij}(y, 0)|+|g^{ij}_{\alpha}(y, z)-g^{ij}_{\alpha}(y, 0)|\lesssim \varepsilon |z|(1+|z|),\\
    \label{e.na.g.approx}
		|\partial_{y_l} g_{\alpha,ij}(y, z)|+ |\partial_{y_k}\partial_{y_l} g_{\alpha,ij}(y, z)|+ |\partial_{y_l} g^{ij}_{\alpha}(y, z)|+ |\partial_{y_k}\partial_{y_l} g^{ij}_{\alpha}(y,z)| \lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^2),\\
    \label{e.gamma.alpha.approx}
        |\Gamma_{\alpha, ij}^k(y,z)-\Gamma_{\alpha, ij}^k(y,0)|\lesssim \varepsilon |z|(1+|z|),\\
    \label{e.partial.gamma.alpha.approx}
        |\partial_{y_l}\Gamma_{\alpha, ij}^k(y,z)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2),\\
                    
                                                                                                             
    \label{e.sff.approx}
		|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha}(y, z)-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha}(y, 0)|\lesssim\varepsilon^2|z|(1+|z|^3),\\
    \label{e.mn.curv.approx}
 		|H_{\alpha}(y, z)-H_{\alpha}(y, 0)|\lesssim\varepsilon^2|z|(1+|z|^3),\\
    \label{e.nablasff}
        \vert\nabla_{\alpha,z}\mathrm{I\!I}_\alpha(y, z)-\nabla_{\alpha, 0}\mathrm{I\!I}_\alpha(y, 0)\vert\lesssim \varepsilon^2|z|(1+|z|^3)\\
    \label{e.vol.form}
		\vert \lambda_\alpha(y, z) - \lambda_\alpha(y, 0) \vert \lesssim \varepsilon |z|(1 + |z|). 
	                                       
		               
			         
			                                                                                                                        
			                                                                                                                                
			             
		                
    \end{gather}    
	with constants depending on $n, K, \delta, \eta_0$ and $\Lambda_0$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
See Appendix \ref{ap:geometric.approx} for the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{l.Lapl.tw.Fer}
Let $T=(T^i)$ be as in Remark \ref{r.tZ-Z}. Then,  if $(y,z)$ denote twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_\alpha$, we have 
\begin{align}\label{e.Lapl.tw.Fer}
	\Delta \varphi = & \Delta_{\alpha, z}\varphi + \partial_{zz}\varphi -H_\alpha(y,z)\partial_z\varphi +\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}(y, z)\varphi
	\end{align}
where 
\begin{align}\label{diff operator E=E1+E2}
\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}(y, z)\varphi
= H_\alpha(y,z) T \ast \partial_y \varphi + T\ast T \ast \partial_{yy}^2\varphi + T\ast \nabla T \ast \partial_y \varphi + \nabla T \ast \partial_y \varphi + T \ast \partial^2_{y,z} \varphi.
\end{align}
In particular, every
coefficient in $\mathscr E_\alpha$ is controlled by \eqref{e.difference.z.tz}.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prope.comparing laplacian}
	Let $K>0$ be fixed. For $\varphi_0\in C^2(\Sigma_{\alpha})$, let $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R))$ be defined as in \eqref{e.const.extension}. Then, there holds
	\begin{equation} \label{e.comparing laplacian}
		|\Delta_{\alpha, z}\varphi-\Delta_{\alpha, 0} \varphi|\lesssim\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)(|\nabla^2_{\alpha, 0}\varphi_0|+|\nabla_{\alpha, 0}\varphi_0|)
	\end{equation}
	for $z\in (-K|\log \varepsilon|, K|\log \varepsilon|)$, where the constant depends on $n, K, \delta, \eta_0$ and $\Lambda_0$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For a general function $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R))$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.lapl.gamma}
\Delta_{\alpha,z}\varphi(y,z)
=\sum_{i,j=1}^ng_\alpha^{ij}(y,z)\partial_{y_iy_j}\varphi(y,z)
-\sum_{i,j,k=1}^ng_\alpha^{ij}(y,z)\Gamma_{\alpha,ij}^k(y,z)\partial_{y_k}\varphi(y,z).
\end{equation}
Thus,
\begin{equation}\label{e.lapl.difference}
\begin{split}
	\Delta_{\alpha, z}\varphi (y,z)-\Delta_{\alpha, 0}\varphi (y,0) &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n(g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,z)-g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0))\partial_{y_i}\partial_{y_j}\varphi(y,z)\\
	&\quad-\sum_{i,j,k=1}^n(g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,z)\Gamma_{\alpha,ij}^k(y,z)-g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)\Gamma_{\alpha,ij}^k(y,0))\partial_{y_k}\varphi(y,z)\\
	&\quad +\sum_{i,j=1}^ng_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)(\partial_{y_i}\partial_{y_j}\varphi(y,z)-\partial_{y_i}\partial_{y_j}\varphi(y,0))\\
	&\quad -\sum_{i,j,k=1}^n g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)\Gamma_{\alpha,ij}^k(y,0)(\partial_{y_k}\varphi(y,z)-\partial_{y_k}\varphi(y,0)).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
In the case where $\varphi$ is the $z$-constant extension of $\varphi_0\in C^2(\Sigma_{\alpha})$ as in \eqref{e.const.extension}, then \eqref{e.partial.constant.extension} holds, and \eqref{e.partial.constant.extension} follows directly from \eqref{e.g_ij.approx} and \eqref{e.gamma.alpha.approx}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{mean curvature expansion tf}
Fix $K>0$.  Let $\varphi\in C^2(\Sigma_\alpha)$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\Sigma_\alpha)}\leq K|\log\varepsilon|,
 \qquad |\nabla_{\alpha,0}\varphi|\leq\eta_0,
 \qquad |\nabla^2_{\alpha,0}\varphi|\leq\Lambda_0\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}
Let $\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]$ denote the graph of $\varphi$ in twisted Fermi coordinates, parametrized by
$y\mapsto Y_{\Sigma_\alpha}(y,\varphi(y))$, and let $H_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}$ denote its mean curvature. 
For each fixed $\varphi$, define an operator on $\psi\in C^2(\Sigma_\alpha)$ by
\[
 \mathcal L_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}\psi(y)
 :=\left[
 \frac{\Delta_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}(\psi\circ\Pi_\alpha)}
 {\langle\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]},\nabla t_\alpha\rangle}
 \right]\!\left(Y_{\Sigma_\alpha}(y,\varphi(y))\right),
\]
where $\psi\circ\Pi_\alpha$ is restricted to the graph before applying its
intrinsic Laplacian.  For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, this is a
linear uniformly elliptic operator in weighted divergence form, and
\[
 \mathcal L_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}1=0,
 \qquad \mathcal L_{\Sigma_\alpha[0]}=\Delta_{\alpha,0}.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 H_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}-H_{\Sigma_\alpha}
 ={}&\mathcal L_{\Sigma_\alpha[\varphi]}\varphi
 +\bigl(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_\alpha}|^2
       +\operatorname{Ric}_g(\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_\alpha},\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_\alpha})\bigr)\varphi
 +\mathcal Q(y,\varphi,d\varphi),
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
where $\mathcal Q(y,z,p)$ is a smooth function of the base point, height,
and covector $p\in T_y^*\Sigma_\alpha$, and satisfies
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 |\mathcal Q(y,\varphi,d\varphi)|
 \leq{}& C\varepsilon|d\varphi|^2
 +C\varepsilon|\varphi|^2
          |\nabla_{\alpha,0}H_\alpha(y,0)|+C\varepsilon^3|\varphi|^2(1+|\varphi|^2).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
The norms on the right are taken with respect to $g_{\alpha,0}$.
The ellipticity constants and $C$ are independent of $\varepsilon$ and
$\alpha$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
See Appendix \ref{ap:geometric.approx}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{p.commutator.laplacian}
Let $K>0$ be fixed. For all $\varphi\in C^3(\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R))$, we have the following commutator estimate 
\begin{equation}\label{e.exchange.derivative}
	|\Delta_{\alpha, z} \partial_{y_i}\varphi-\partial_{y_i}\Delta_{\alpha, z}\varphi|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2)(|\nabla^2_{\alpha, z}\varphi|+|\nabla_{\alpha, z}\varphi|)
\end{equation}
for $z\in (-K|\log \varepsilon|, K|\log \varepsilon|)$.
The constant depends on $n, K, \delta, \eta_0$ and $\Lambda_0$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Using the formula in \eqref{e.lapl.gamma}, we see that
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
    \Delta_{\alpha, z} \partial_{y_i}\varphi-\partial_{y_i}\Delta_{\alpha, z}\varphi &= -\sum_{j,k=1}^n(\partial_{y_i}g_{\alpha}^{jk})\partial_{y_j}\partial_{y_k}\varphi+\sum_{j,k,l=1}^n\left((\partial_{y_i}g_{\alpha}^{jk})\Gamma_{\alpha,jk}^l+g_{\alpha}^{jk}(\partial_{y_i}\Gamma_{\alpha,jk}^l)\right)\partial_{y_l}\varphi
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where all terms are evaluated at $(y,z)$. Then \eqref{e.exchange.derivative} follows from \eqref{e.g_ij.approx},
\eqref{e.na.g.approx},
\eqref{e.gamma.alpha.approx}, and \eqref{e.partial.gamma.alpha.approx}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
Let $K>0$ be fixed. For all $\varphi\in C^3(\mathbb{B}^+_{1.6R}(0)\times (-2R,2R))$, we have the following commutator estimates
\begin{align}
    \label{e.exchange.zneumannderivative0}
        |\partial_{z}\partial_{\nu}\varphi-\partial_{\nu}\partial_{z}\varphi|&\lesssim \varepsilon{(1+|z|)}|\nabla \varphi|,\\
    \label{e.exchange.1neumannderivative0}
        |\partial_{\nu}\partial_{y_1}\varphi-\partial_{y_1}\partial_{\nu}\varphi|&\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^2)|\nabla \varphi|,\\
    \label{e.exchange.neumannderivative0}
        |\partial_{\nu}\partial_{y_i}\varphi-\partial_{y_i}\partial_{\nu}\varphi|&\lesssim \varepsilon |z|  (1+|z|)|\nabla \varphi|\;\text{ for all $2\leq i\leq n$}
                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                          
                                                                                                                                                                              
                                         
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                          
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
\end{align}
on $\partial_0\{|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}$.
The constants depend on $n, K, \delta, \eta_0$ and $\Lambda_0$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Recall that $\nu=\partial_{x_1}$ on $\partial_0\{|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}$. Thus, $\partial_{z}\partial_{\nu}\varphi-\partial_{\nu}\partial_{z}\varphi=[Z, \partial_{x_1}]\varphi$. If we write $Z=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}Z^k\partial_{x_k}$, then $[Z, \partial_{x_1}]=-\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_1}Z^k)\partial_{x_k}$, and \eqref{e.exchange.zneumannderivative0} follows directly from \eqref{e.na.Z}.

Now, let $L_i\coloneqq [\partial_{x_1}, \partial_{y_i}]$, so that \eqref{e.exchange.1neumannderivative0} and \eqref{e.exchange.neumannderivative0} amount to estimating $L_i$ for $i=1, 2, \dots, n$.\\ Let $L_i|_{(y,z)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}L_i^k(y,z)\partial_{x_k}|_{(y,z)}$.
On $\partial_0\Sigma_\alpha$, $\partial_{y_i}|_{(y,0)}=\partial_{x_i}|_{(y,0)}+\partial_{x_i}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)}$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}
    [\partial_{x_1}, \partial_{y_i}]|_{(y,0)}=\partial_{x_1}\partial_{x_i}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)} = \partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_1}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)}.
\end{equation}
If $i=1$, for $(y,0)\in \partial_0\Sigma_\alpha$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{e.Y_1(0)}
|L^k_1(y,0)|\lesssim\Lambda_0\varepsilon
\end{equation}
 for all $k=1, \dots, n+1$ by \eqref{e.na.f}.
On the other hand, if $2\leq i\leq n$, then by the Neumann condition for $f$ on $\partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{2R}(0)$, if $(y,0)\in \partial_0\Sigma_\alpha$. 
\begin{equation}\label{e.Y_i(0)}
    L^k_i(y,0)=0
\end{equation}
 for all $k=1, \dots, n+1$.

We now want to estimate $L_i^k(y,z)$ by deriving the ODE it satisfies.

Since $\partial_{y_i}, \partial_z$ are coordinate vectors $[Z, \partial_{y_i}]=0$ everywhere. Moreover, by direct computation $[Z,L_i]=[[Z,\partial_{x_1}], \partial_{y_i}]$, i.e.
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
    \partial_zL_i^k = [Z, L_i]^k+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_j}Z^k)L_i^j
    =[[Z,\partial_{x_1}], \partial_{y_i}]^k+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_j}Z^k)L_i^j.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Let us write $\partial_{y_i}|_{(y,z)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n+1}b_i^m(y,z)\partial_{x_m}|_{(y,z)}$, where $b_i^m(y,z)=\partial_{x_i}\Theta_m(z,y)+\partial_{x_i}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}\Theta_m(z,y)$ by \eqref{e.del_y_i}.
We have
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
    [[Z,\partial_{x_1}], \partial_{y_i}]^k=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}b_i^j(\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_1}Z^k)-(\partial_{x_j}b_i^k)(\partial_{x_1}Z^j).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Hence, the functions $L_i^k$ satisfy an ODE system of the form 
\[\partial_zL_i^k(y,z) = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1}c_j(y,z)L_i^j(y,z)+d_i^j(y,z),\]
where the coefficients satisfy $|c_j(y,z)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|)$ and $|d_i^j(y,z)|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|)$ by \eqref{e.na.Z}.
By Gronwall's inequality for vector valued functions \cite[Theorem D.2]{Lee}
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
    |L_i(y,z)|\lesssim \exp(\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|))(|L_i(y,0)|+\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Therefore, for $|z|<K|\log\varepsilon|$, $|L_i(y,z)|\lesssim |L_i(y,0)|+\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)$,
which implies \eqref{e.exchange.1neumannderivative0} and \eqref{e.exchange.neumannderivative0}, by \eqref{e.Y_1(0)} and \eqref{e.Y_i(0)} respectively.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{l.projection.error}
	For any $K>0$, there is a constant $C(K)$ so that for $\alpha\not= \beta$, $x\in \mathbb{B}_{2R}^+(0)\times (-2R,2R)$ with $|t_{\alpha}(x)|, |t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log \varepsilon|$, 
	\begin{align}
		\label{e.proj.1}
		d_{\Sigma_ {\beta}}(\Pi_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\alpha}(x), \Pi_{\beta}(x)) &\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}\\
		\label{e.proj.2}
		|t_{\beta}(\Pi_{\alpha}(x))+t_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(x))|&\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}\\
		\label{e.proj.3}
		|t_{\alpha}(x)-t_{\beta}(x)+t_{\beta}(\Pi_{\alpha}(x))|&\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}\\
		\label{e.proj.4}
		|t_{\alpha}(x)-t_{\beta}(x)-t_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(x))|&\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}\\
		\label{e.proj.5}
		\left|1-\langle\nabla t_{\alpha}(x),\nabla  t_{\beta}(x)\rangle\right|&\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}
	\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The proof is a simple modification of \cite[Lemma 8.3]{wang-wei} (or, more precisely, its Riemannian version in \cite[Lemma B.1]{chodosh-mantoulidis}), thanks to Lemma \ref{l.Fc.vs.tFc.1} and Lemma \ref{l.Fc.vs.tFc.2}, which show that, under the current assumptions, the twisted Fermi coordinate time functions $t_\alpha, t_\beta$ coincide with the corresponding Fermi distance functions $\tilde{t}_\alpha, \tilde{t}_\beta$, and that the twisted Fermi projection maps $\Pi_\alpha, \Pi_\beta$ are comparable to the corresponding Fermi projection maps $\tilde{\Pi}_\alpha, \tilde{\Pi}_\beta$, up to a small error of order $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^3$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{p.conseq.almost.parallel}
Let $x$ be as above and assume it has twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_\alpha$.
Then the following estimates hold:
\begin{align}\label{eq:tb-tb0}
	&t_\beta(y,z) = t_\beta(y,0)+z+o(\varepsilon^{1/3})\\
\label{e.partial_zt_beta}
    &|\partial_z t_\beta-1|\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/3}\\
\label{0Dalphaztbeta}
	&|\nabla_{\alpha, z} t_\beta|\lesssim \varepsilon^{\frac{1}{5}}\\
\label{nabla2alphaztbeta}
    &|\nabla^2_{\alpha,z}t_\beta|\lesssim \varepsilon
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
The exponents appearing in \eqref{eq:tb-tb0}, \eqref{e.partial_zt_beta}, and \eqref{0Dalphaztbeta} are not sharp. Indeed, as it is apparent from the proof, from Proposition \ref{l.projection.error}, we can obtain
\begin{align*}
    &t_\beta(y,z) = t_\beta(y,0)+z+O(\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2})\\
    &|\partial_z t_\beta-1| \lesssim \varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2}\\
    &|\nabla_{\alpha, z} t_\beta| \lesssim \varepsilon^{1/4}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/4}\\
\end{align*}
In particular, some of the exponents appearing e.g. in \eqref{horizontalphicontrolh} and in some other estimates of the later section could be slightly improved. This however does not seem to significantly affect the final results.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
First, notice that by \eqref{e.proj.4}, after swapping $\alpha$ and $\beta$, if $x$ has twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_\alpha$, then by a slight abuse of notation, we can write $t_\beta(y,z)=t_\beta(y,0)+z+O(\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2})$.
In particular, for all $\theta\in(0,1/2)$ and all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ (depending on $K$ and $\theta$)
\begin{equation}
	t_\beta(y,z)=t_\beta(y,0)+z+o(\varepsilon^{1/2-\theta})
\end{equation}
provided $|t_\beta(y,z)|, |z|\leq K |\log \varepsilon|$. This proves \eqref{eq:tb-tb0}.

Next, notice that at $x$, since $|\nabla t_\beta|=1$,
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			|\partial_z t_\beta-1| &= |\langle\nabla t_\alpha+(\partial_z-\nabla t_\alpha), \nabla t_\beta\rangle-1|=|\langle \nabla t_\alpha, \nabla t_\beta\rangle-1+\langle \partial_z-\nabla t_\alpha, \nabla t_\beta\rangle|\\
			&\leq |\langle \nabla t_\alpha, \nabla t_\beta\rangle-1|+|\langle \partial_z-\nabla t_\alpha, \nabla t_\beta\rangle|\\
			&\lesssim \varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2} + \varepsilon(|t_\alpha(x)|+|t_\alpha(x)|^2)\\
			&\lesssim \varepsilon^{1/2}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/2} + \varepsilon (|\log \varepsilon|+|\log \varepsilon|^2)\\
			&\lesssim \varepsilon^{1/2-\theta}
		\end{split}
	\end{equation}
	for any $\theta\in(0,1/2)$, by Lemma \ref{l.Z.Z-tld} and Proposition \ref{l.projection.error}, which implies \eqref{e.partial_zt_beta}.

    Similarly,
	\begin{equation}
		|\nabla_{\alpha, z}t_\beta|\lesssim|\nabla t_\beta-\langle\nabla t_\beta, \nabla t_\alpha\rangle \nabla t_\alpha| \!=\!\sqrt{1-\langle \nabla t_\alpha, \nabla t_\beta \rangle^2}\leq \sqrt{2(1-\langle \nabla t_\beta, \nabla t_\alpha\rangle)}\lesssim \varepsilon^{1/4}|\log \varepsilon|^{3/4}
	\end{equation}
	by \eqref{e.proj.5}. In particular, $|\nabla_{\alpha, z} t_\beta|\lesssim \varepsilon^{1/4-\theta}$ for any $\theta\in(0,1/4)$, thus proving \eqref{0Dalphaztbeta}.

    Next, notice that $\nabla_{\alpha, z}^2t_\beta=\nabla^2 t_\beta+\langle \nabla t_\beta, \nabla t_\alpha\rangle \mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha, z}$. Since $t_\beta=\tilde t_\beta$, then $\nabla^2 t_\beta$ is precisely the second fundamental form of $\Sigma_{\beta, t_\beta}$. Recall that by \eqref{e.na.f}, $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha, 0}|=O(\varepsilon)$ and $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\beta, 0}|=O(\varepsilon)|$. Since we are assuming $|t_\alpha(x)|, |t_\beta(x)|\leq K|\log \varepsilon|$, by \eqref{e.sff.approx}, 
	\[|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha, 0}| = |\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha, t_{\alpha}(x)}-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,0}|\lesssim \varepsilon^2|\log\varepsilon|^4,\]
	so that $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha, z}|=O(\varepsilon)$, and, similarly, $|\nabla^2 t_\beta|=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\beta,t_\beta(x)}|=O(\varepsilon)$. Hence, by \eqref{e.proj.5}, \eqref{nabla2alphaztbeta} holds.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{l.DPi.beta}
Let $K>0$ be fixed. Let $(y, z)$ be twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$, and let $\Pi_\beta$ denote the twisted Fermi coordinate projection map with respect to $\Sigma_\beta$. 
Then,
\begin{equation}\label{e.Dpi.bound}
    |D\Pi_\beta(\partial_{y_i})|=O(1)
\end{equation}
for $i=1, \dots, n$, and
\begin{equation}\label{e.Dzpi.bound}
    |D\Pi_\beta(\partial_{z})|\lesssim \varepsilon^{\frac{1}{5}}
\end{equation}
uniformly in the region where $|t_\alpha|, |t_\beta|\leq K|\log \varepsilon|$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Equation \eqref{e.Dpi.bound} follows from Lemma \ref{l.t.Pi}.  For
\eqref{e.Dzpi.bound}, write $Z_\gamma$ and $\widetilde Z_\gamma=\nabla t_\gamma$ for the twisted
and ordinary Fermi fields associated with $\Sigma_\gamma$.  The projection $\Pi_\beta$ is constant
along the flow of $Z_\beta$, and hence $D\Pi_\beta(Z_\beta)=0$.  Since
$\partial_z=Z_\alpha$ in the $\alpha$-coordinates,
\[
 D\Pi_\beta(\partial_z)=D\Pi_\beta(Z_\alpha-Z_\beta).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 Z_\alpha-Z_\beta
 =(\widetilde Z_\alpha-\widetilde Z_\beta)
 +(Z_\alpha-\widetilde Z_\alpha)-(Z_\beta-\widetilde Z_\beta).
\]
The first term is $O(\varepsilon^{1/4}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/4})$ by
\eqref{e.proj.5}, while the last two are $O(\varepsilon(|\log\varepsilon|+|\log\varepsilon|^2))$
by Lemma \ref{l.Z.Z-tld}.  Combining these estimates with the uniform bound for $D\Pi_\beta$
gives \eqref{e.Dzpi.bound}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{l.del.y_1.t_be 2} There holds
\begin{equation}
	|\nabla^m \mathsf{J}_{\alpha \beta}|\lesssim \varepsilon(1+|z|^3+ |t_{\beta}| + t_{\beta}^2) \; \text{ on } \partial_0\{x:|t_{\alpha}(x)|, |t_{\beta}(x)| \leq K |\log \varepsilon|\}\quad \forall  m \ge 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
We note that
	\begin{equation}
		\mathsf{J}_{\alpha \beta} = \langle \nabla t_{\beta} , \partial_{y_1} - \partial_{x_1} \rangle + J_{\beta}
	\end{equation}
	Since $\partial_{x_1}=\partial_{y_1}$ along $\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}$, it follows from Lemma \ref{l.na.y_i} that 
	\begin{equation}
		|\nabla^m (\partial_{x_1}-\partial_{y_1})|\lesssim \varepsilon(1 +|z|^3)\;\text{ on }\partial_0\{|z|\leq K|\log \varepsilon |\}\quad \forall m\ge 0.
	\end{equation}
Using Lemma \ref{l.dz(nu)} in the form $J_\beta=w_\beta t_\beta+\widetilde J_\beta$, the apparently cubic part of the crude bound is absorbed by
$\varepsilon^2|t_\beta|^2(1+|t_\beta|^3)\leq C_K\varepsilon$ in the logarithmic strip.  Together with the preceding estimate and Lemma \ref{l.t.Pi}, this gives the stated bound for $\mathsf J_{\alpha\beta}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{l.sum.of.exp}
	For any $y\in \Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\sigma > 0$, we have 
	\begin{equation}\label{exponential sum1}	
		\sum_{\beta\not=\alpha}e^{- \sigma|t_{\beta}(y)|}\lesssim_{K, \sigma} e^{- \sigma D_{\alpha}(y)},  
	\end{equation}
	uniformly with respect to $y$ and $\alpha$. For  $x\in \mathcal{M}^{4}_{\alpha}$ with $|t_\alpha(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$, we have 
	\begin{equation}\label{exponential sum2}
		\sum_{\beta\not=\alpha}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(x)|}\lesssim_{K, \sigma} e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha+1}(x)|}+e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha-1}(x)|}
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{l.1D.soln}
	Let $\varepsilon_i>0$ be a sequence\ which converges to $0$, $R_i=\varepsilon_i^{-1}$, $u_i(x):=u_{\varepsilon_i}(\varepsilon_ix)$, $x_i\in \{u_i=0\}\cap (\mathbb{B}^+_{R_i}(0)\times (-R_i, R_i))$, $\Sigma_{x_i}$ be the connected component of $\{u_i=0\}$ in $\mathbb{B}^+_{R_i}(0)\times (-R_i, R_i)$, which contains $x_i$. Suppose\ in  twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to\ $\Sigma_{x_i}$, $x_i=(y_i,0)$, $\tilde{u}_i(y,z):= u_i(y_i+y,z)$ and $u_i(y,z)$ has the same sign as $z$. Then, up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_i(y,z)$ converges to $\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^3_{\text{loc}}$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The proof is similar to \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}. Suppose\ in  twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to\ $\Sigma_{x_i}$, $x_i=(y_{i,1},\dots, y_{i,n},0)$. When $\liminf_{i\rightarrow \infty}y_{i,1}=\infty$, $\tilde{u}_i$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.ac.1} on $B_{y_{i,1}}(0)$, $\tilde{u}_i(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)=0$ and $\partial_z\tilde{u}_i(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)\geq 0$. By the elliptic estimates, $\tilde{u}_i$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{4}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$. Therefore, there exists\ $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$, a stable solution of \eqref{e.ac.1} on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, such that\ up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_i\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)=0$ and $\partial_z\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)\geq 0$. As explained in \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}, since $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies \eqref{e.esff.bd}, there holds $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b'\}\cap \{|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$. By the unique continuation principle, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a lift of $\mathbb{H}$; hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,z)=\mathbb{H}(z)$.
	
	If $\liminf_{i\rightarrow \infty}y_{i,1}<\infty$, then, possibly after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that $y_{i,1}$ is uniformly bounded. Let $x'_i=(y'_i,0)=(0,y_{i,2},\dots, y_{i,n},0)$ (which is a point in $\partial_0\mathbb{B}^+_{R_i}(0)\times (-R_i, R_i)$). We define $\hat{u}_i(y,z)=u_i(y'_i+y,z)$. Then $\hat{u}_i$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.ac.1} on $B^+_{R_i}(0)$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial_0B^+_{R_i}(0)$, $\hat{u}_i(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)=0$ and $\partial_z\hat{u}_i(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)\geq 0$. $\hat{u}_i$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{4}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$. Hence there exists\ $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$, a stable solution of \eqref{e.ac.1} on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial \mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+$, such that\ up to a subsequence, $\hat{u}_i\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$, $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)=0$ and $\partial_z\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,0)\geq 0$. We extend $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by even reflection (as in \eqref{e.even.refl}). Then $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a stable solution of \eqref{e.ac.1}. Since $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies \eqref{e.esff.bd}, arguing as in \cite[Proof of Lemma 2.1]{wang-weiadv}, we conclude that $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b'\}\cap \{|\nabla \tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$. By the unique continuation principle, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a lift of $\mathbb{H}$; hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_1,\dots,y_n,z)=\mathbb{H}(z)$. Thus $\hat{u}_i(y,z)\rightarrow\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+)$. Since $y_{i,1}$ is uniformly bounded, this implies $\tilde{u}_i(y,z)\rightarrow\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{l.D_al.infty}
	As $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$, $\inf\limits_{\alpha}\inf\{D_{\alpha}(y):y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap (\mathbb{B}^+_R(0)\times (-R,R)) \} \rightarrow +\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The proof of \eqref{exponential sum1} is identical to the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.6]{wang-weiadv}, with Lemma \ref{l.D_al.infty} replacing \cite[Lemma 2.2]{wang-weiadv}, and Proposition \ref{l.projection.error} replacing \cite[Lemma 3.4]{wang-weiadv}. Then, \eqref{exponential sum2} follows directly from \eqref{exponential sum1}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:maing}We have
\begin{align}\label{eq:maing}
(\Delta_{\alpha,0}+\partial_z^2-W''(\mathbb{H}_\alpha))\mathbb{G}_\alpha
 ={}&|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_\alpha|^2\mathbb{G}_\alpha^{(2)}
 -(-1)^\alpha(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_\alpha)\mathbb{G}_\alpha^{(1)}\notag\\
 &-2(-1)^\alpha\sum_{i,j}g_\alpha^{ij}(y,0)
       \mathbb{G}'_{\alpha,i}\,\partial_{y_j}h_\alpha+\xi_{2,\alpha},
\end{align}
\begin{align}\label{eq:main}
 (\Delta_{\alpha,0}+\partial_z^2-W''(\mathbb{H}_\alpha))\mathbb{G}_\alpha^{(1)}
 ={}&|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_\alpha|^2\mathbb{G}_\alpha^{(3)}
 -(-1)^\alpha(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_\alpha)\mathbb{G}_\alpha^{(2)}\notag\\
 &-2(-1)^\alpha\sum_{i,j}g_\alpha^{ij}(y,0)
       \mathbb{G}''_{\alpha,i}\,\partial_{y_j}h_\alpha+W'''(\mathbb{H}_\alpha)\mathbb{H}_\alpha^{(1)}\mathbb{G}_\alpha+\xi'_{2,\alpha}.
\end{align}
\begin{align}
    \partial_{y_1}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)+(-1)^{\alpha}w_{\alpha}(y)\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)z &= \delta_{\alpha}\label{Neumanny1 G0}\\
\partial_{y_1 y_i}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)+(-1)^{\alpha} \partial_{y_i}w_{\alpha}(y)\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)z &= \delta_{\alpha, i} \quad (2\leq i\leq n). \label{Neumanny1yi G0}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{l.interaction.int}
Let $K>0$ be fixed, let $\beta\neq\alpha$ satisfy
$|t_\beta(y,0)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$, and let
$\sigma,\varsigma\geq0$ with $\sigma+\varsigma>0$.  For every $k\in\mathbb N$,
\begin{align}\label{equation 3 in l.interaction.int}
 \int_{-K|\log\varepsilon|}^{K|\log\varepsilon|}
 |z|^ke^{-\sigma|t_\beta(y,z)|-\varsigma|z|}\,dz
 &\lesssim (1+|t_\beta(y,0)|)^{k+1}
 e^{-\min\{\sigma,\varsigma\}|t_\beta(y,0)|},\\
\label{equation 1 in l.interaction.int}
 \int_{-K|\log\varepsilon|}^{K|\log\varepsilon|}
 |t_\beta(y,z)|^ke^{-\sigma|t_\beta(y,z)|-\varsigma|z|}\,dz
 &\lesssim (1+|t_\beta(y,0)|)^{k+1}
 e^{-\min\{\sigma,\varsigma\}|t_\beta(y,0)|}.
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{l.interaction.int.2}
Let $K>0$ be fixed.  If $\beta\neq\alpha$ and
$|t_\beta(y,0)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{equation 2 in l.interaction.int}
 \int_{\mathbb R}
 \left|\overline{\mathbb{H}}(t_\beta(y,z))+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)\right|
 |\overline{\mathbb{H}}'(z)|\,dz
 \lesssim (1+|t_\beta(y,0)|)e^{-|t_\beta(y,0)|}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $\sigma\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.interaction.sigma.correct}
 \int_{\mathbb R}
 \left|\overline{\mathbb{H}}(t_\beta(y,z))+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)\right|
 |\overline{\mathbb{H}}'(z)|\,dz
 \lesssim_\sigma e^{-\sigma|t_\beta(y,0)|}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def.notation.balls}
For $\bar x=(\bar y,f_\alpha(\bar y))\in\Sigma_\alpha$ set
\[
 B_r^\alpha(\bar x)=\{(y,f_\alpha(y)):y\in\mathbb B_{2R}^+(0),\ |y-\bar y|<r\}.
\]
For $\bar x\in\partial_0\Sigma_\alpha$ set
\[
 B_r^{0,\alpha}(\bar x)=\{(y,f_\alpha(y)):y\in\partial_0\mathbb B_{2R}^+(0),\ |y-\bar y|<r\}.
\]
Their relative closures are $\bar B_r^\alpha(\bar x)$ and $\bar B_r^{0,\alpha}(\bar x)$.
The notation with centre $\bar y$ has the same meaning under the graph parametrization.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{r.ball.comparison}
    Notice that, by \eqref{e.rescaled.bound.gEucl} and \eqref{e.na.f}, it is easy to see that for all small enough $\eta_0$ (independent of $\varepsilon$), the coordinate balls $B^\alpha_r(\cdot)$,  $B^{0,\alpha}_r(\cdot)$ are uniformly comparable to the (intrinsic) geodesic balls in $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}$ respectively. In particular, it is easy to check that there are constants $c_0(n), c_1(n)$ such that for all sufficiently small $\eta_0$, 
    \begin{equation}
        B^\alpha_{(1-c_1(n)\eta_0)r}(x)\subset B^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}_r(x)\subset B^\alpha_{(1+c_1(n)\eta_0)r}(x) \ \text{ for all } x\in \Sigma_{\alpha},
    \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation}
        B^{0,\alpha}_{(1-c_0(n)\eta_0)r}(x)\subset B^{\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}}_r(x)\subset B^{0,\alpha}_{(1+c_0(n)\eta_0)r}(x) \ \text{ for all } x\in \partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha},
    \end{equation}
    where $B^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}_r(x)$ (resp. $B^{\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}}_r(x)$) denotes the open geodesic ball of radius $r$ centred at $x$ in $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}$).
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Much like in Remark \ref{r.ball.comparison}, notice that, again by by \eqref{e.rescaled.bound.gEucl} and \eqref{e.na.f}, up to a harmless dimensional constant, for all small enough $\eta_0$ (independent of $\varepsilon$) and all $S\subset \Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $S\subset \partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}$), $\sup_{x\in S}|\varphi|_{0,\theta}(x)$ is uniformly comparable to the H{\"o}lder seminorm $[\varphi]_{\theta, S}$ defined using the intrinsic distance on $\Sigma_{\alpha}$. Similarly for $\sup_{x\in S}|\varphi|_{j,\theta}(x)$ and $[\nabla^j\varphi]_{\theta, S}$. 
    
    Therefore, after taking $\eta_0$ sufficiently small (independent of $\varepsilon$), we can use appropriate suprema of the quantities in \eqref{j-theta norm} to define the H{\"o}lder seminorms.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{p.optimal_h_shift}
	There exists $h_{\alpha}\in C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$ such that for each index $\alpha$ and $y\in \Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)$, for $\phi(y, z; h)=u(y, z)-\mathbb{H}(y, z; h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)$ there holds
	\begin{equation}\label{e.ortho.H'_al}
	\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\phi(y, z; h)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_\alpha)dz=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y, z)-\mathbb{H}(y, z; h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_\alpha)dz=0,
	\end{equation}
where $(y,z)$ are twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$. Moreover, the following estimates hold uniformly with respect to\ the index $\alpha$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.h=o1 stronger} 
\begin{aligned}
		& |h_{\alpha}|_{j} + |h_{\alpha}|_{j, \theta} \lesssim \varepsilon + \omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9},\; 0\leq j \leq k, \text{ on } \Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0),\\ 
	&|\partial_{y_1}h_{\alpha}|_{(j-1)} + |\partial_{y_1}h_{\alpha}|_{(j-1),\theta} \lesssim (\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha} + \mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9})(\varepsilon + \mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(j)} + \mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}),\; 1\leq j \leq k,  \text{ on }\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{r.optimal_h_shift}
    In later application, we will fix $k=3$ and $j=2$ in Proposition \ref{p.optimal_h_shift}, so that $h_{\alpha}=o(1)\in C^{3,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$. In this case, for ease of notation, we write (compare with \eqref{notation wwaa})
    \begin{equation}\label{m=m2, w=w2}
        \mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}=\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(2)}\qquad \text{and} \qquad \omega_{\alpha}=\omega_{\alpha}^{(2)}.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, we can simplify the estimate \eqref{e.h=o1 stronger} satisfied by $h_{\alpha}$ in Proposition \ref{p.optimal_h_shift} to  
 \begin{equation}\label{e.h=o1}
\begin{aligned}
	& \sum_{i=0}^2 |h_{\alpha}|_{i} + |h_{\alpha}|_{2,\theta}\lesssim \varepsilon + \mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}\text{ on } \Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0),\\ 
	&\sum_{i=0}^1|\partial_{y_1}h_{\alpha}|_{i}+|\partial_{y_1}h_{\alpha}|_{1,\theta}\lesssim \varepsilon^2+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^2+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{1.8}    \text{ on }\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
To this end, we shall modify the proof in \cite[Proof of Proposition 4.1]{wang-weiadv} as follows. For each $k$ and $\theta\in (0, 1)$ and $\alpha$, we define new norms $\|\cdot\|_{*}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\star}$ on $C^{k, \theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{9R/10}(0))$ and $C^{k, \theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{R}(0))$. We introduce $\|\mathfrak{h}\|_{*}:=\sum_{j=0}^k [\mathfrak{h}]_{*;j} + \sum_{j=1}^k [\mathfrak{h}]'_{*;j}$, where
\begin{align}
	& [\mathfrak{h}]_{*;j}=\Lambda^{-1} \sup_{\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)}  \frac{|\mathfrak{h}|_{j} + |\mathfrak{h}|_{j,\theta} }{\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}},\\
	& [\mathfrak{h}]'_{*;j}=\Lambda^{-2}\sup_{\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)} \frac{|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1)}+|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1),\theta}}{(\varepsilon +\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}) (\varepsilon+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(j)}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9})},
\end{align}
$\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}$ denotes the restriction of $\partial_{y_1}\mathfrak{h}$ on $\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}$, $\Lambda > 1$ is a constant, which will be specified later. Let us denote \( \bar{\mathscr{R}}(\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha})\), \(\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathrm{a}_{\alpha})\), \(\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha})\), and \(\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha})\) by \(\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha} \), \(\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha} \), \(\bar{\mathfrak{w}}_{\alpha} \), and \(\bar{\mathfrak{a}}_{\alpha} \), where restriction map $\bar{\mathscr{R}}$ is defined in \eqref{restriction map}.
$\|\mathfrak{h}\|_{\star}:=\sum_{j=0}^k[\mathfrak{h}]_{\star;j} + \sum_{j=1}^k [\mathfrak{h}]'_{\star; j}$, where
\begin{align}
	& [\mathfrak{h}]_{\star; j}=\Lambda^{-1} \sup_{\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0)}  \frac{|\mathfrak{h}|_{j} + |\mathfrak{h}|_{j,\theta} }{\varepsilon+\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9}}, \\
	& [\mathfrak{h}]'_{\star; j}=\Lambda^{-2} \sup_{\partial_0\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0)} \frac{|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1)}+|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1),\theta}}{(\varepsilon +\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9}) (\varepsilon+\bar{\mathfrak{w}}_{\alpha}^{(j)} + \bar{\mathfrak{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9})}.
\end{align}
 






Following \cite[Proof of Proposition 4.1]{wang-weiadv}, we define 
$$\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}=(C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{R}(0)),\|\cdot\|_{\star}),\quad \mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}=(C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{9R/10}(0)), \|\cdot\|_{*}),$$
$\mathcal{X}=\bigoplus_{\alpha}\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}$, $\mathcal{Y}=\bigoplus_{\alpha}\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$. The norm on $\mathcal{X}$ is defined by $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\sup_{\alpha}\|\mathbf{x_{\alpha}}\|_{\star},$ where $\mathbf{x_{\alpha}}$ is the $\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}$ component of $\mathbf{x}$. The norm on $\mathcal{Y}$ is defined in a similar way. 


Recall the definition of $g_{\beta}(y, z;h_{\beta})$ and $g(y, z; h)$  from \eqref{def_gk=H+G} and \eqref{def_g=H+G}. Then we define $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ by
\begin{align}
    F_{\alpha}(h)(y)&=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y, z)-g(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_{\alpha})dz\\
    &=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y, z)-\mathbb{H}(y, z; h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_{\alpha})dz,
\end{align}
where $F_{\alpha}(h)$ denotes the $\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ component of $F(h)$ and $(y,z)$ denotes the twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$. We restrict $F$ on the closed unit ball in $\mathcal{X}$. We note that, for $y\in \Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\mathsf{y}\in \bar{B}_1^{\alpha}(y)$,
\((g_{\beta}(\mathsf{y},z;h_{\beta})+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta - \alpha)(-1)^{\beta}) \mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(\mathsf{y}, z; h_{\alpha}) \neq 0\), $\beta \neq \alpha$, implies \(|z|< 9 |\log \varepsilon|\) and \(\beta \in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}\);  hence

\begin{equation}
	F_{\alpha}(h)(\mathtt{y})=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\big[u(\mathtt{y}, z)-g_{\alpha}(\mathtt{y}, z; h_{\alpha})-\sum_{\beta\in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}} (g_{\beta}(\mathtt{y},z;h_{\beta})+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta - \alpha)(-1)^{\beta})\big] \mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(\mathtt{y}, z; h_{\alpha})dz.
\end{equation}

Notice that $F$ is a $C^1$ map, and its derivative $(DF_{\alpha}(h)\xi)(y)$ is given by
		\begin{align}\label{e.DF_alpha}
		 & (-1)^{\alpha}\xi_{\alpha}(y)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; h_{\alpha})^2+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; h_{\alpha})\right]dz\\
		 & - (-1)^{\alpha}\xi_{\alpha}(y)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[u(y, z)-\mathbb{H}(y, z; h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)\big]\mathbb{H}''_{\alpha}(y, z; h_{\alpha})dz\\
		& +\sum_{\beta\in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}(-1)^{\beta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\xi_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z))\mathbb{H}_{\beta}'(y, z; h_{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_{\alpha})dz\\
		& +\sum_{\beta\in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}(-1)^{\beta} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\xi_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z))\mathbb{G}'_{\beta}(y, z; h_{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}'(y, z; h_{\alpha})dz.
	\end{align}
	Thus, there exist continuous\ linear maps $D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(h):\mathcal{X}_{\beta}\to \mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ such that
	\[DF_{\alpha}(h)\xi=D_{\alpha}F_{\alpha}(h)\xi_{\alpha}+\sum_{\beta\in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(h)\xi_{\beta}.\]
	Let $\mathsf{T} = DF(0)$, $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}=D_{\alpha}F_{\alpha}(0)$, $\mathsf{T}_{\beta\alpha}=D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(0)$ for $\beta\not=\alpha$. Then, $(\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}\xi_{\alpha})(y)=\vartheta_{\alpha}(y)\xi_{\alpha}(y)$, where 
	\begin{align}\label{e.expr.vth}
		\vartheta_{\alpha}(y) = & (-1)^{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left[\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)^2+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}'(y, z;0)\mathbb{H}'_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)\right]dz\\
		& -(-1)^{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[u(y, z)-\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)-\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)\big]\mathbb{H}''_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)dz\\
		&+(-1)^{\alpha}\sum_{\beta\in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y, z; 0)+\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(y,z;0)\big]\mathbb{H}''_{\alpha}(y, z; 0)dz.
	\end{align}

\begin{claim}\label{c.DF.F}	
We have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
	\item There exists\ $DF(0)^{-1}$, which is a right inverse of $DF(0)$, such that\  the operator norm of $DF(0)^{-1}$ satisfies  $\|DF(0)^{-1}\|\leq C(\sigma_0)$, where $\sigma_0$ is the energy of the one-dimensional solution, as in \eqref{e.sigma0}.
	\item $h \mapsto DF(h)$ is Lipschitz continuous\ at $h=0$ and its Lipschitz constant at $0$ is $ \Lambda c_{\varepsilon}$, where $c_{\varepsilon}=o(1)$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$.
	\item $\|F(0)\|_{\mathcal{Y}}\leq C \Lambda^{-1}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.	 
\end{enumerate}
\end{claim}	

First, let us assume Claim \ref{c.DF.F} and let us finish the proof of Proposition \ref{p.optimal_h_shift}. We will show  the existence of $h\in \mathcal{X}$ satisfying \eqref{e.ortho.H'_al} and estimates \eqref{e.h=o1 stronger} by the contraction mapping principle, as in \cite[Theorem 1.2.4]{chang2005methodsnonlinear}.

Note that it is enough to show that there exists\ $h\in \mathcal{X}$ such that\ $\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1$ and $F(h)=0$.  Let $\mathsf{R}:\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_1(0)}\to \mathcal{Y}$ be defined by $\mathsf{R}(h)=F(h)-DF(0)h$. $F(h)=0$ if and only if $DF(0)h=-\mathsf{R}(h)$. Let $\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h):=-DF(0)^{-1}\mathsf{R}(h)$. If $h$ is a fixed point of $\bar{\mathsf{R}}$, then $F(h)=0$. 

We note that
\begin{equation}
	\mathsf{R}(h)-\mathsf{R}(\tilde{h})=\int_{0}^{1} \left(DF(\gamma(t))-DF(0)\right)(h-\tilde{h})dt,\;\text{ where }\gamma(t) = th+(1-t)\tilde{h}.
\end{equation}
Hence, denoting the Lipschitz constant of $DF$ at $0$ by $\Lambda c_{\varepsilon}$ ($c_{\varepsilon}=o(1)$ as \(\varepsilon\to 0\)) and using (i) and (ii) of Claim \ref{c.DF.F}, 
\begin{equation}\label{e.R.bar.1}
	\|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h)-\bar{\mathsf{R}}(\tilde{h})\| \leq C(\sigma_0)\Lambda c_\varepsilon \|h-\tilde{h}\|,
\end{equation}
which implies
\begin{equation}\label{e.R.bar.2}
	\|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h)\| \leq C(\sigma_0) \Lambda c_\varepsilon \|h\|+\|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(0)\|.
\end{equation}
By  (i) and (iii) of Claim \ref{c.DF.F}, we  can fix $\Lambda$ sufficiently large so that 
\begin{equation}
    \|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(0)\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq  1/2.
\end{equation}
Then, \eqref{e.R.bar.1} and \eqref{e.R.bar.2} imply that if $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, $\bar{\mathsf{R}}:\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_1(0)}\to\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_1(0)}$ is a contraction. Hence, $\bar{\mathsf{R}}$ has a fixed point $h$ in $\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_1(0)}$ satisfying estimates \eqref{e.h=o1 stronger} and $F(h)=0$. This finishes the proof of Proposition \ref{p.optimal_h_shift}.

Let us now prove Claim \ref{c.DF.F}.

                                                

\noindent\textit{\textbf{Proof of (i).}} 
As a preliminary to the construction of a right inverse of $DF(0)$ satisfying the required operator norm estimate, we shall establish the following two facts:
\begin{enumerate}[(a):]
    \item There exists $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}:\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}\to\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}$, which is a right inverse of $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}$, such that\ the operator norm of $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}$ satisfies $\|\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}\|\leq C(\sigma_0)$.
    \item The operators $\mathsf{T}_{\beta\alpha}:\mathcal{X}_{\beta}\to\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ for $\beta\neq \alpha$ satisfy $\|\sum_{\beta \in \mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y} }\mathsf{T}_{\beta\alpha}\xi_{\beta}\|_{*; 3, \theta}=o(1)\|\xi\|_{\mathcal{X}}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
                                                                                                                                  
\end{enumerate}


\noindent\textit{\textbf{Proof of (a).}}  Let $\mathscr{R}:C^{3, \theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{9R/10}(0))\to C^{3, \theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^+_{7R/8}(0))$ denote the restriction map. By \cite[Lemma 6.37]{gilbarg1977elliptic},  there exists\ an extension operator $\mathscr{R}^{-1}$, which is a continuous right inverse of $\mathscr{R}$. 

By Lemmas \ref{l.1D.soln}, \ref{l.interaction.int}, \ref{l.D_al.infty}, \ref{l.sum.of.exp} and \eqref{e.G.est}, 
\begin{equation}\label{e.vth.lower.bd}
|\vartheta_{\alpha}(y)|\geq \frac{\sigma_0}{2}.
\end{equation}
Then we can define the right inverse of $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}$ by $(\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}\eta_{\alpha})(y):=\vartheta_{\alpha}(y)^{-1}\tilde{\eta}_{\alpha}(y)$ where $\tilde{\eta}_{\alpha}=\mathscr{R}^{-1}{\eta_{\alpha}}$.  We need to show that $\|\vartheta_{\alpha}^{-1}\tilde{\eta}_{\alpha}\|_{\star}\leq C(\sigma_0) \|\eta_{\alpha}\|_{*}$. Again by Lemmas \ref{l.1D.soln}, \ref{l.interaction.int}, \ref{l.D_al.infty}, \ref{l.sum.of.exp} and \eqref{e.G.est}, we also have
\begin{equation}\label{e.vth.bd}
